entries.title: On Copaganda
entries.html:
I really wonder how much of the internet-based media (which is pretty much the only way I get my shows and stories, lately) that I consume is either indirectly or directly sponsored by organisations and institutions which I am strongly morally opposed to. I have a sneaking suspicion that it is more than I would like to think.

Take law enforcement for example, and the proliferation of so called "procedural dramas" like Law And Order and the excessive number of spin-offs and sequels, all following the same formula: ripped-from-the-headlines dramatisations loosely based on real world events, told from the perspective of various roles in the criminal justice system. These shows slip in pro-law-enforcement themes and ideas at every turn. It's sort of subtle, but mixed with a fair amount of emotional manipulation and dramatic twists, it doesn't really even have to be that sneaky. It's a very entertaining formula and one that, i imagine, practically writes itself.  

About 15 years ago I was in a bit of a depressive rut, although I lacked the self awareness and perspective at the time to realize it. After a breakup which I should have seen coming a mile and a couple months away, and didn't take very well, I filled my days by lying around the house feeling sorry for myself and drinking. If that sounds boring as hell, it's because it was, and so to keep myself from going nuts or becoming even more depressed, I started binge watching Law And Order. I liked the regularity of it, the predictability, and, in hindsight, it provided a semblance of structure and regularity that I lacked in all other areas of my life. I watched all 22 seasons, back to back. It took me about 3 months of nothing but lying in bed, mindlessly passively absorbing pro-police falsehoods and glorifying the horribly broken criminal justice system. What can I say, it was addictive. The recurring characters were like my friends, not unlike the low level drug dealers I would find myself latching on to a couple of years later (they're not really your friends, but it's close enough to keep you from feeling completely alone and turning to the friends and family who have been avoiding watching you wallow in the misery of your own making.)

Is it any wonder that shortly after I finished that series, and coinciding with the debut of another one called "Breaking Bad" (maybe you've heard of it?), which I didn't get past the second or third season of, was when I started a rather steep  descent into my former life as an aspiring career criminal. I guess young people really are as impressionable as they say. I certainly didn't see that coming. They say hindsight is 20/20, but personally I say it is a curse, since we cannot change the past, why must we be unnecessarily burdened with the knowledge of what we should have done instead? Except for the gift of the choice of whether or not to repeat your mistakes over and over. 

Hindsight is the lens through which regret is focused to a white-hot pin-point that burns the ego. 

... but back to my point about the state of entertainment today, and who is behind the rise of "true crime" and "dark and mysterious stories" genre that has become wildly popular on streaming platforms like youtube and tiktok. How much of that stuff is being put out there by pro-law-enforcement interests? The likely answer is,  a lot. Most of it? Nearly all?

I wish I knew... as if it was even possible to quantify, transparency about such things is, I fear, at an all time low and probably not bound to improve any time soon. Increasingly I feel as though I am being advertised to in more and more places that I used to feel I could trust to deliver me relatively unbiased information (or, at least, not secretly sponsored and with a hidden agenda).

Make no mistake: this genre, of which I am an admitted fan, is Copaganda, and it is nothing like the reality of the criminal justice system. I believe it exists to convince us that we need the police more than we do. It is a whitewash of an institution which has been in desperate need of sweeping reform and more restraints for decades, even the better part of a century now. 

Since I have no plans to curb my consumption of this type of content, the best I can hope to do is consume it with a critical and mindful eye on the messages and subtle themes and biases that pervade it, and stay cognisant of how they contradict the reality of the world we live in; the one in which America is, unfortunately, rapidly becoming an authoritarian surveillance state. If you had told me as a teenager, pre-911, that this is where we were headed, I probably wouldn't have believed you.

But then, I was a pretty gullible as a kid.

entries.title: Procedural Art
entries.html:
What is programming, really? It's something I have loved to do for as long as I can remember, there are few things that bring me as much joy and satisfaction as the indirect act of creating something devilishly complex by sequencing some deceptively simple (we say "elegant") instructions for this universal machine, then watching it compute and chug along happily turning bits of entropy into bits of answers and pixel-perfect isometric worlds where every problem has a whole number solution and there's nothing that can't be accomplished in polynomial time (if you look at it from the right point of view, at least.)

Most of my life I have felt like an artist, but seen as an engineer or technician, someone whose work is devoid of expression or emotion or soul. But there is so much artistry in technology and engineering... there is even a kind of spiritualism in electric circuits (if you get really into analog design) and RF is just spooky, even once you understand how it can be that a vibrating current in a wire here can cause an identical one on the other side of the planet (or deep in outer space, for that matter.) The magic of that is undeniable. There is so much art in technology, yet nobody looks at programming as an art, because it is a science, and science and art are naturally opposed. How untrue!

I am a procedural artist. My medium is the language of the machine: it accepts the instructions that I carefully craft out of thin air (and an idea of what it is I wish to create) and then it runs my program and produces via it's simple step-by-step execution the final product, the work that the audience can interact with.
